content: Endometriomas are ovarian cysts caused by endometriosis, and their presence may interfere with the outcomes of assisted reproductive technology (ART) cycles, as these procedures involve retrieving oocytes from the ovaries. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of various interventions, including surgical, medical, combination therapies, or no treatment, in improving reproductive outcomes for women with endometriomas prior to undergoing ART. The authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases and sources, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Register of trials, CENTRAL, EMBASE, MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, DARE, trial registries, citation indexes, conference abstracts, and other resources. The search was last updated in July 2010. They also manually reviewed issues of the journal Fertility and Sterility from 2008 to 2010. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating medical, surgical, combination therapies, or expectant management for endometriomas prior to ART were included in the analysis. Two authors independently assessed the trials for eligibility and risk of bias. Additional information was sought from the authors of potentially eligible studies. The outcomes of interest were expressed using Peto odds ratios and mean differences (MD). A total of 11 trials were identified, but only four trials involving 312 participants met the inclusion criteria. Seven trials were excluded. None of the included trials reported live birth outcomes. One trial compared the use of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists with GnRH antagonists. While there was no significant difference in the clinical pregnancy rate (CPR) between the two groups, the number of mature oocytes retrieved (NMOR) was higher in the GnRH agonist group (MD -1.60, 95% CI -2.44 to -0.76). Additionally, ovarian response, as measured by estradiol (E2) levels on the day of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) injection, was greater in the GnRH agonist group (MD -456.30, 95% CI -896.06 to -16.54). When comparing surgical interventions (aspiration or cystectomy) to expectant management (EM), there was no evidence of a benefit in terms of clinical pregnancy rates with either technique. However, aspiration was associated with a higher NMOR (MD 0.50, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.98) and an increased ovarian response, as indicated by higher E2 levels on the day of hCG injection (MD 685.3, 95% CI 464.50 to 906.10), compared to EM. In contrast, cystectomy was associated with a reduced ovarian response to controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) (MD -510.00, 95% CI -676.62 to -343.38) and showed no significant effect on the NMOR compared to EM. When comparing aspiration to cystectomy, there was no evidence of a difference in CPR or NMOR between the two surgical techniques. The authors concluded that there was no evidence of an effect on reproductive outcomes in any of the four included trials. They emphasized the need for further randomized controlled trials to evaluate the management of endometriomas in women undergoing ART.
